With his sister's remains in front of him, Jiang Wei's hands began to tremble. He feared the spade's sharp edge might harm her bones. But at least he still had his hands.

"Easy now. Don't hurt yourself," came a soft voice beside him. A cool palm covered his, threading a rare warmth into the rain-soaked night.

Jiang Wei paused, then turned.

The woman beside him was someone he had rescued not long ago from a ghost marriage. For years, he had disguised himself as a bride to infiltrate such dark rites, saving women from the clutches of the Ghost Matchmakers, searching always for the one behind his sister's death. This woman... her brows and eyes bore a faint resemblance to his sister's. So when she offered to come with him, Jiang Wei did not refuse. Turns out, it was much-needed company for him.

Along the way, she had held the umbrella for him against the rain, halted his reckless strides through blizzards, listened quietly as he recounted his past, and calmed him down when rage threatened to consume him. Without her, his fraying mind might have already shattered.

"Thank you... for everything you've done for me along the way." Jiang Wei scooped another handful of earth. "Once I bring my sister to the sea, I'll see you safely home."

As he dug, pale bones came into view. Jiang Wei froze, a half-smile tugging at his lips, half joy, half grief.

"The freedom my sister longed for... This time, I'll give it to her."

But no answer came. The oil-paper umbrella slipped from his shoulder and fell to the ground. Jiang Wei turned around, there was nothing but silence behind him.

Pain ripped through him. Memories flashed before his eyes, then shattered into dust. There had never been anyone. On this long, twisted, bloodstained road, he had always walked alone.

Jiang Wei curled up beside his sister's bones, staring up at the rain pouring from the heavens. 

If all the warmth, all the companionship he believed in was but a lie. Then what in this world was ever real?

The people he had saved. The ones he had killed. Everything he had seen, everything he had endured, was it all just a dream spun out of his own madness?

Jiang Wei closed his eyes. After a few shallow breaths, he let out a faint, broken laugh.

There was once an elderly woman brought to the Evercare Clinic. Her children had long since moved to Kaifeng, and when illness struck, there was no one left to care for her. The villagers, helpless and unsure of what else to do, brought her to the clinic. When she saw Doudou—the boy who delivered her medicine—she smiled and pressed a handful of sweet candies into his palm. He reminded her of her grandson. No one knew why, but from that day on, Doudou visited her every day. He would sit by her side, chat with her, and make her laugh. When Yaoyao asked him why, Doudou simply replied, "She's kind. Maybe... maybe she's someone I lost—a relative, maybe." Yaoyao knew the truth: Doudou had no family. He was an orphan, taken in by Unfated Tian. But Unfated Tian had made it clear—never say that in front of the boy. So Yaoyao simply sighed and let it go.

Doudou believed that Unfated Tian could cure anyone. He was the greatest healer in the world, and surely he could make the elderly woman well again. But only a month later, she passed away.

Unfated Tian found Doudou sitting alone by the pond, his arms wrapped tightly around his knees. Unfated Tian sat beside him and spoke gently, "Birth, aging, illness, and death... they're all part of life's path." But Doudou didn't understand. If death came no matter what, then what was the point of being a healer? Unfated Tian didn't answer. Instead, he reached into his sleeve and pulled out a small paper-wrapped bundle—candies. "She knew her time was short," Unfated Tian said, "But you made her laugh. You made her less afraid. These were her way of saying thank you."Doudou took the bundle in his small hands, and for the first time since she'd gone, he cried.
